newsitem.title: GERMANY: BUDGET ISSUES TO TOP AGENDA AT FRANCO-GERMAN TALKS.
newsitem.headline: BUDGET ISSUES TO TOP AGENDA AT FRANCO-GERMAN TALKS.

text.p: Germany, fresh from pushing a package of controversial spending cuts through parliament, is likely to spur on its closest European neighbour France to do the same when the countries' financial leaders meet on Tuesday.

Germany's Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer will join their French counterparts in the Bavarian town of Kempten on Tuesday morning for a regular half-day meeting of the Franco-German economic council.

The meeting, sandwiched between critical budget talks in Bonn and Paris, also falls just three days ahead of an informal meeting of European Union finance officials in Dublin, Ireland which will address key aspects of the single currency project.

Germany and France, the two countries unanimously regarded as indispensible founder members of the planned European currency, will agree their joint position for the Dublin talks in the framework of broader economic discussions.
But one source familiar with Bonn's position on European Economic and Monetary Union said there were unlikely to be any major new European initiatives emerging from Kempten.
He dismissed financial market talk of a stronger currency link between the French franc and the German mark, which regularly precedes such bilateral meetings, as unrealistic.
"I would expect the usual outcome," he said.

Such Franco-German meetings regularly end with an upbeat summary of each country's growth prospects, optimism jobless figures will fall and above all a reaffirmation of their joint determination to make the single currency a success.
This time around, with budget shortfalls seen as the main obstacle to the timely creation of the Euro in 1999, the urgent need for public spending cuts will be high on the agenda.
The Maastricht Treaty -- which sets goals on interest and exchange rates, inflation and public budgets -- calls for Euro nations to have deficits of no more than three percent in 1997.

Germany, the self-appointed guardian of Europe's fiscal discipline, is already aiming well below that level, and will hope to inspire France's financial leaders with the confidence to adopt hardline measures in the face of public protest.

Waigel heads for Kempten with parliamentary approval for three key bills in his pocket, giving him a confidence boost to implement a budget which aims to bring Germany's deficit well below three percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in 1997.

But the French government, which is due to present its budget on Wednesday, is already showing signs of flagging in its determination to push such measures through, harried by negative public opinion and the threat of widespread strikes.

The 1997 budget, which aims to bring the total public deficit to within three percent of GDP from a targeted four percent this year, contains substantial spending cuts, but is much less harsh than many had expected.
Instead, one-off revenue, including a transfer of 37 billion francs ($7.17 billion) to cover France Telecom pensions, will be used to help it reach the three percent goal.
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer last week indirectly criticised such window-dressing, making clear that fiscal stability was not simply a question of juggling figures.

But while Germany is likely to frown publicly on such tactics, the Bonn source said it may well accept them tacitly in the final assessment providing France's budget, along with its own, sets a clear standard of relative excellence.
